title: CASE WHEN
objective: Turn raw values into business labels with CASE, count and sum conditionally with SUM(CASE ...), and write CASE expressions that handle NULL on purpose.
context: Merchandising wants price tiers, finance wants orders bucketed by size, and leadership wants a one-row-per-year scorecard with completed, cancelled and pending orders side by side. All of these are the same tool: a CASE expression placed in SELECT, inside an aggregate, in GROUP BY or in ORDER BY.

exercises.title: Price tiers that don't lose NULLs
exercises.question: Merchandising wants every product tagged with a price tier for the catalog review.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, list_price and price_tier for all 25 products. price_tier is 'Unpriced' when list_price is NULL, 'Budget' when list_price < 30, 'Mid' when list_price is 30 up to (but not including) 100, otherwise 'Premium'.
hints: Branches are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, so put the NULL check first.
WHEN list_price < 100 only runs for rows that already failed < 30, so it means 30–99.99.
CASE WHEN list_price IS NULL THEN 'Unpriced' WHEN list_price < 30 THEN 'Budget' WHEN list_price < 100 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Premium' END AS price_tier
exercises.why: Product 19 has no price. Without the explicit NULL branch it falls through every comparison to ELSE and gets labelled 'Premium', which is a wrong label that nobody would notice.

recall.q: What does a CASE without ELSE return for a row that matches no WHEN?

exercises.snowflake: Same CASE syntax. For a two-way split you could write IFF(list_price < 30, 'Budget', 'Other').

exercises.title: Revenue vs excluded orders
exercises.question: Finance wants a quick count of orders that count for revenue versus those that don't.
exercises.prompt: Return status_group and order_count. status_group is 'Revenue' for valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) and 'Excluded' for every other status. Count all orders in the table (including the orphan order 31).
hints: Build the label with CASE, then GROUP BY that label.
IN (...) works inside WHEN just like in WHERE.
SELECT CASE WHEN order_status IN (...) THEN 'Revenue' ELSE 'Excluded' END AS status_group, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY status_group;
exercises.why: Grouping by a derived label is how you collapse messy source codes into the handful of buckets a business actually reports on.

recall.q: Can you GROUP BY a CASE expression?
recall.a: Yes. Repeat the expression or (in SQLite/Snowflake) use its alias or position.

exercises.title: Bucket orders by size
exercises.question: The ops team wants each valid order labelled Small / Medium / Large by its value.
exercises.prompt: For each valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) return order_id, order_total = SUM(quantity * unit_price) rounded to 2 decimals, and size_bucket: 'Small' when the (unrounded) total is < 100, 'Medium' when < 300, otherwise 'Large'.
hints: Join orders to order_items, filter valid statuses, GROUP BY order_id.
A CASE can test an aggregate: WHEN SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) < 100 THEN ...
SELECT o.order_id, ROUND(SUM(...), 2) AS order_total, CASE WHEN SUM(...) < 100 THEN 'Small' WHEN SUM(...) < 300 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Large' END AS size_bucket FROM ... GROUP BY o.order_id;
exercises.why: Size buckets drive shipping rules, fraud review thresholds and marketing segments. CASE over an aggregate is evaluated per group, after GROUP BY.

recall.q: Can CASE wrap an aggregate like SUM(...)?
recall.a: Yes. In a grouped query, CASE WHEN SUM(x) < 100 ... is evaluated once per group.

exercises.title: Yearly order scorecard (conditional aggregation)
exercises.question: Leadership wants one row per year showing how many orders were valid, cancelled and pending.
exercises.prompt: Return order_year (strftime('%Y', order_date)), total_orders (all orders), valid_orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), cancelled_orders and pending_orders. Use every row in orders.
hints: One GROUP BY year; each status becomes its own column.
SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts rows that meet a condition.
SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders — repeat for valid and pending.
exercises.why: Conditional aggregation is how a 'pivot' gets written in plain SQL. One pass over the table replaces three separate filtered queries.

recall.q: Name two ways to count only cancelled orders inside a grouped query.
recall.a: SUM(CASE WHEN order_status='cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), or COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE order_status='cancelled') (Snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status='cancelled')).

exercises.snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled_orders; YEAR(order_date) AS order_year.

exercises.title: Category revenue, 2024 vs 2025 side by side
exercises.question: The category managers want this year's and last year's revenue next to each other.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return category (NULL category shown as 'Uncategorized'), revenue_2024 and revenue_2025 (by order_date year), each rounded to 2 decimals and showing 0 rather than NULL if a category had no sales that year.
hints: Join orders → order_items → products and keep valid orders only.
Inside SUM, return the line value for the target year and 0 otherwise.
ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024' THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue_2024
exercises.why: Year-over-year columns are the most requested layout in business reviews. 'ELSE 0' vs no ELSE decides whether an empty year shows 0 or NULL, and dashboards treat those differently.

recall.q: In SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN x END) with no ELSE, what is the result if no row matches?
recall.a: NULL, because SUM over only NULLs is NULL. Add ELSE 0 to get 0.

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake also offers PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR order_year IN ('2024','2025')), but conditional aggregation is portable and easier to control.

exercises.title: Customer loyalty segments (including non-buyers)
exercises.question: CRM wants every customer, including ones who never bought, placed in a loyalty segment.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, valid_order_count (number of valid orders: valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and segment for all 20 customers: 'Inactive' for 0 valid orders, 'One-time' for 1, 'Repeat' for 2–4, 'Loyal' for 5 or more.
hints: Customers without orders must survive, so this needs a LEFT JOIN from customers.
Put the status filter in the ON clause (a WHERE would drop the non-buyers), and COUNT(o.order_id) so missing matches count 0.
... LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name — then CASE on COUNT(o.order_id).
exercises.why: Segments that silently drop non-buyers under-count your reactivation audience. Customer 16 (only a cancelled order) is 'Inactive', not missing.

recall.q: Why COUNT(o.order_id) instead of COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN?
recall.a: COUNT(*) counts the NULL-extended row as 1; COUNT(o.order_id) ignores NULLs and gives 0.

exercises.title: Status counts in lifecycle order
exercises.question: The ops dashboard lists statuses in lifecycle order, not alphabetically.
exercises.prompt: Return order_status and order_count (all orders), sorted in lifecycle order: pending, shipped, completed, returned, cancelled.
hints: ORDER BY can sort by any expression, including a CASE that maps statuses to numbers.
A simple CASE fits: CASE order_status WHEN 'pending' THEN 1 WHEN 'shipped' THEN 2 ... END
GROUP BY order_status ORDER BY CASE order_status WHEN 'pending' THEN 1 ... WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 5 END;
exercises.why: Business orderings (funnel stages, size tiers, weekdays) are rarely alphabetical. A CASE sort key keeps the sort in the query instead of in someone's spreadsheet.

recall.q: How do you sort rows in a custom, non-alphabetical order?
recall.a: ORDER BY a CASE expression that maps each value to its rank.

worked_example.question: How many orders are in each lifecycle group, and how many of them count for revenue?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped') THEN 'fulfilled'
            WHEN order_status = 'returned'               THEN 'returned'
            ELSE 'not fulfilled'
       END                                          AS lifecycle_group,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                  AS revenue_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY lifecycle_group;
worked_example.explanation: The first CASE builds a label and GROUP BY groups on it (SQLite lets you reference the alias; Snowflake does too). The second CASE sits *inside* SUM: each row contributes 1 or 0, so the sum is a conditional count. 'not fulfilled' = 5 cancelled + 2 pending, and they contribute 0 revenue orders.

recipe:
**Recipe: label, then aggregate the label**

1. **Searched CASE** — the general form. Branches are tested top to bottom; the *first* true one wins:
   ```sql
   CASE WHEN list_price IS NULL THEN 'Unpriced'   -- handle NULL first, on purpose
        WHEN list_price < 30    THEN 'Budget'
        WHEN list_price < 100   THEN 'Mid'
        ELSE 'Premium'
   END AS price_tier
   ```
   Because branches are ordered, `< 100` already implies `>= 30` — no need for BETWEEN.
2. **Simple CASE** — compares one expression with values: `CASE order_status WHEN 'completed' THEN 1 ... END`.
   It uses `=`, so `WHEN NULL` never matches. Use a searched `WHEN col IS NULL` instead.
3. **No ELSE → NULL.** A row that matches nothing gets NULL. With an ELSE, NULL inputs silently fall into
   the ELSE bucket (a NULL price would be called 'Premium'!). Decide where NULL goes.
4. **Conditional aggregation** — put CASE *inside* the aggregate to pivot statuses/years into columns:
   ```sql
   SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                 AS cancelled_orders,
   SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2025' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS amount_2025
   ```
   `ELSE 0` gives 0 instead of NULL when nothing matches. (SQLite also has `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)`.)
5. **CASE anywhere an expression goes**: `GROUP BY` a bucket, or `ORDER BY CASE ... END` for a custom sort order.
snowflake_notes:
- `CASE` is identical in Snowflake. Snowflake also has `IFF(cond, a, b)` (SQLite: `IIF(cond, a, b)`) for
  two-way choices, and `DECODE(expr, v1, r1, v2, r2, default)` — note that DECODE *does* treat NULL = NULL as a match.
- Conditional counts: `COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled')` is Snowflake shorthand for
  `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
- `DIV0(a, b)` / `DIV0NULL` avoid division-by-zero errors that you would otherwise guard with CASE.
common_mistakes: Leaving NULL out of the plan: with an ELSE, NULL inputs fall into the ELSE bucket; without one, the label is NULL.
Writing `CASE col WHEN NULL THEN ...`. Simple CASE uses =, which never matches NULL. Use `CASE WHEN col IS NULL`.
Overlapping or out-of-order branches (`WHEN x < 300` before `WHEN x < 100`): the first true branch wins, so 'Small' is never reached.
Forgetting `ELSE 0` inside SUM(CASE ...) and getting NULL instead of 0 for empty buckets.
Filtering a LEFT JOIN's right table in WHERE, which turns it back into an inner join and drops the 'Inactive' customers.
recall: What's the difference between a simple CASE and a searched CASE?
Simple: CASE expr WHEN value THEN ... (equality only). Searched: CASE WHEN condition THEN ... (any predicate, including IS NULL).
An aggregate whose input is a CASE, e.g. SUM(CASE WHEN status='cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), turning rows into pivoted columns.
Where can a CASE expression appear?
Anywhere an expression can: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, inside aggregates.
